content: Scrub typhus, also known as Bush typhus, is a type of typhus caused by the intracellular parasite Orientia tsutsugamushi. This organism is a Gram-negative α-proteobacterium belonging to the family Rickettsiaceae. It was first isolated and identified in Japan in 1930. While the clinical presentation of scrub typhus resembles other forms of typhus, its causative pathogen is no longer classified within the genus Rickettsia alongside the traditional typhus bacteria. Instead, it is categorized under the genus Orientia. Consequently, scrub typhus is often classified separately from other typhus diseases. During a physical examination, typical clinical signs of scrub typhus include a maculopapular rash, the presence of an eschar (a necrotic skin lesion at the site of the mite bite), splenomegaly (enlargement of the spleen), and lymphadenopathies (swollen lymph nodes). In endemic regions, the diagnosis of scrub typhus is generally made based on clinical findings alone. However, in cases where there is diagnostic uncertainty, confirmation can be achieved through laboratory testing, such as serological assays.
